chapter: New York, Philadelphia and Harlem nightlife
title: Clash By Night: Billy Rose and the search for a second pianist
summary: Tallulah Bankhead supports Price; Billy Rose hires him for a primitive blues score and tries many pianists, settling on Arthur Gibbs.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Tallulah was quite a jazz fan, wasn't she...
Yep. She was one of my staunch supporters. She liked blues and she liked jazz. She loved Sidney Bechet.
I used to see them together.
Yeah. She loved Sidney. But I could play that thing that...Did I tell you how I got...I did the Tallulah Bankhead
No. You said you were in it. That was Clash By Night

Clash By Night. Well, what happened was, Billy Rose called Barney Josephson and asked him to have me come up to the Diamond Horseshoe. And they wanted...they had a scene... the theme of the thing was they wanted a blues, you know what I mean, like "Rhapsody in Blue." Not that kind of thing but th suggested, you know, kind of thing, you know, blues throughout, you know, that blues mood, and sad, and tragic... lonesome music.

So Billy Rose wasn't at the Diamond Horseshoe. They asked me to come over to his house on Sutton Place. So I went over to Billy's house and we became like father and son, or brother...two brothers. So he says, "Sam, now I'll tell you. I don't care what happens, you got the job." He wanted two piano players. "You got one of the jobs. Don't worry." He said, "No matter what you see me do, or what I do, don't you worry." Do you know that he called at least a hundred piano players to play with me? James P. Johnson, Willie the Lion Smith, Donald Lambert , Meade Lux Lewis, Pete Johnson, da, da and da. But what he wanted, primarily, was a guy that could read some little notes and cues, that's what he wanted. He wanted an untrained piano player.
Billy was...oh, he was some showman. 'Course, wait 'til I tell you what Tallulah Bankhead did to him. He wanted untrained sound. He wanted it to be primitive,

and this is what I was playing. But he wanted that other piano player to be able to play with me, which would show a contrast, yet it would be similar, or it could work together. So here we come...we tried everybody...James P.--I thought James P. was going to get it. And Willie 'the Lion,' I thought he was going to get it...I thought they was going to go by the name of a person, you know, but they finally ended up selecting Arthur Gibbs, the man that wrote "Running Wild."
